messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nadia is a 46-year-old single Iranian-American pharmacist who presented for an initial psychological evaluation reporting significant distress that she traced back to a medical crisis involving her daughter approximately two years prior. At that time, her then-nine-year-old daughter was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit following a sudden and severe septic episode. Nadia had been the first to notice that something was wrong — her daughter's lips had taken on a grayish tint during what had seemed like an ordinary evening at home — and she had driven to the emergency department herself, watching in the rearview mirror as her daughter slipped in and out of consciousness. The weeks that followed were defined by the sounds of ventilators, the smell of antiseptic corridors, and the particular pitch of cardiac monitors alarming in the night. Her daughter ultimately survived and recovered fully, but Nadia had not.

In the months following discharge, Nadia found herself unable to return to any version of the life she had known before. She had come to believe, with a quiet but absolute conviction, that she was fundamentally defective — that a competent mother, a competent pharmacist, a competent person would not have been so undone by something her child had survived. She was certain there was something broken in her that others could not see, and that nothing of real value lay ahead for her. These beliefs did not remain inert. They pressed her toward action: she began working to push all memory of the crisis out of conscious awareness, trying hard not to think about it whenever images surfaced, and she found herself spending long stretches of time turning the question over — why had this happened to her, what had she done, what did it mean. The appraisals themselves seemed to generate a kind of vigilance, a low-grade but continuous sense that the world remained dangerous in ways she could not afford to ignore.

Nadia works as a pharmacist at a large retail pharmacy, a setting that has become one of the primary arenas in which her distress plays out. She reviews medication orders involving pediatric dosing several times a day, and the clinical language on those labels — the names of antibiotics she had seen hung in her daughter's IV lines — can stop her mid-task. She had quietly rearranged her workflow to avoid handling the section of the dispensary that stocked the drugs most associated with that hospitalization. More broadly, she had stopped attending her own annual physical examination, had not entered a hospital building since her daughter's discharge, and changed the route she drives to work to avoid passing the medical center where the admission had taken place. She understood, on some level, that these adjustments were not rational. But each time she tried to relax her guard, her body would not cooperate — she remained unable to unwind even at home in the evenings, startling at ordinary sounds like a car door slamming or a phone ringing in another room, and lying awake well past midnight with a vigilance she could not switch off.

What had become most difficult to bear was the way these patterns fed back into her sense of herself. Her avoidance had cost her: she had declined a promotion that would have required her to consult directly with hospital pharmacy teams, and a close friendship had frayed after she cancelled a series of plans without adequate explanation. Each of these losses confirmed what she already feared — that she was weak, that she was damaged, that she had been permanently diminished. The thought suppression she relied on provided no real relief; the memories returned with force after each effort to contain them, and their return felt like further evidence of her defectiveness. The hypervigilance that kept her awake at night made the next day harder to manage, which in turn deepened her avoidance and her conviction that she was not coping as a person of normal strength would. The loop had been tightening for nearly two years before she sought help.

What finally brought Nadia to the clinic was a panic response she experienced at the pharmacy counter when a customer described a child who had recently been hospitalized. She had excused herself, gone to the staff bathroom, and sat on the floor for twenty minutes. She came to the intake appointment hoping, she said quietly, that she might one day be able to do her job without fear — though she was not sure she believed that was still possible for someone like her.
